newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK civil servants lose battle to join China body.
newsitem.headline: HK civil servants lose battle to join China body.

text.p: Senior Hong Kong civil servants lost a major court battle on Thursday when they failed to reverse a ban on them helping China appoint the new political elite to run the territory after Beijing's mid-1997 takeover.
The group said afterwards they would consider whether to flout the ban and enter the political arena anyway.
The dispute over civil service neutrality is the latest bump along the road to the transfer of sovereignty to China in 292 days' time, when London hands its colony back to Beijing.

"I have come to the conclusion that the restrictions imposed by the government by excluding the senior civil servants is both reasonable and rational," judge Raymond Sears told the High Court in handing down his ruling.
"Some civil servants must recognise the loss of some rights enjoyed by the public is a small price to pay to ensure the integrity of the civil service and to ensure good government."

A lawyer for the more than 1,000 affected civil servants, Gerard McCoy, had argued that the government was behaving in a "schizophrenic" way, as it had allowed 99.3 percent of the territory's 180,000 civil servants -- the junior grades -- to enter the political race for seats in a body that will help shape the new leadership of the territory, but not the 0.7 percent in the top echelon.

But the government argued that a conflict of interest would arise if senior civil servants joined the 400-strong Selection Committee which is to pick Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader and members of a new "provisional legislature".
"I am very pleased about the court decision," Deputy Secretary for the Civil Service Michael Stone told reporters.
The defeated plaintiffs said they would meet later to decide whether to disobey the ban and enter the political contest.

"The judge said it's a small price to pay. We feel it is not a small price to pay. This is a very big price. This is a fundamental civil right at stake. That's why we are greatly disappointed," group spokesman Hui Kwok-Hung told reporters.
Asked if they would appeal, he said this would be meaningless as the deadline for nominations is on Saturday.
The colonial government opposes one of the Selection Committee's main tasks -- the appointment of a provisional legislature to replace the current elected Legislative Council.
China wants to dismantle the legislature on the grounds that the democratic process which elected it last year breached Sino- British treaties on the handover, set for midnight next June 30.
The government has said it wants to preserve the political neutrality of the civil service.

Nominations for Selection Committee seats close at the weekend after a month-long process managed by a 150-member China-controlled panel. The panel, known as the Preparatory Committee, will choose which nominees get the seats. However, the mechanism for this has not been made clear, arousing criticism from pro-democracy groups that the system is undemocratic and inadequately transparent.
The process does not bar servants of the present government. But the civil servants risk losing their jobs if they breach the colonial government's ban on joining the nomination contest.
